description: Programming a processor in its own language: registers, instruction encoding, addressing modes, the stack, interrupts and the bus that connects the CPU to memory and devices. Taught to the depth of a leading machine-level programming and computer organisation course.
modelledOn: Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design (RISC-V edition)
Bryant and O'Hallaron, Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (machine-level chapters)
Mazidi, Causey and Naimi, The x86 PC: Assembly Language, Design and Interfacing
outcomes: Describe the register set, buses, flags and instruction cycle of a microprocessor and the role of each pin and signal.
Decode and encode instructions and choose the right addressing mode for a data access.
Write assembly programs with arithmetic, logic, branching, loops and subroutines that follow a calling convention.
Use the stack for calls, locals and interrupts, and write an interrupt service routine.
Interface memory and I/O devices to a processor with address decoding and polling or interrupts.
Assemble, link, trace and debug programs, and relate compiled C to the assembly it produces.

units.title: Microprocessor architecture and registers
topics: Von Neumann and Harvard architectures; CPU, memory and I/O on address, data and control buses
Inside the CPU: ALU, general-purpose and special registers, program counter, stack pointer, flags
The fetch-decode-execute cycle; clock, machine cycles and timing diagrams
Case processors: the 8086/x86 family, ARM Cortex-M and RISC-V compared; choosing one for the labs
Running programs in a simulator or on a real board; the assembler and debugger toolchain

units.title: Instruction formats and addressing modes
topics: Instruction fields: opcode, operands, immediates; fixed and variable length encodings
Machine code by hand: encoding and decoding a few instructions
Addressing modes: immediate, register, direct, indirect, indexed, base-plus-offset, PC-relative
Data in memory: endianness, alignment, segments or flat memory
Accessing arrays and structures with addressing modes

units.title: Data movement, arithmetic and logic instructions
topics: MOV, loads and stores; constants and labels; data directives
ADD, SUB, ADC, SBB, INC, DEC, NEG; multi-word arithmetic with the carry flag
MUL, IMUL, DIV, IDIV and their quirks; signed versus unsigned
AND, OR, XOR, NOT, TEST; shifts and rotates; masking and bit manipulation
Flags after each instruction; comparing and setting
BCD and ASCII arithmetic; converting numbers to printable strings

units.title: Branching, loops and subroutines
topics: Unconditional and conditional jumps; translating if-else and switch
Loops: counted, while and do-while patterns; loop instructions
CALL and RET; passing arguments in registers and on the stack; return values
Calling conventions: caller- and callee-saved registers, stack frames, recursion
String and block instructions; writing strlen, strcpy and a bubble sort in assembly
Reading compiler output: how C becomes assembly

units.title: Stack and interrupts
topics: Stack organisation, PUSH and POP, stack overflow and underflow
Local variables and the frame pointer
Interrupt types: hardware, software, exceptions; the interrupt vector table
Interrupt sequence: saving state, the service routine, returning; priorities and nesting
Writing an interrupt handler for a timer or key press
System calls on Linux or DOS: writing to the console and exiting

units.title: Memory and I/O interfacing
topics: Memory map and address decoding with gates and decoders; RAM and ROM chips on the bus
Memory-mapped versus port-mapped I/O; IN and OUT
Parallel I/O with the 8255 or a GPIO port; LEDs, switches, seven-segment displays
Serial I/O with a UART; timers and counters
Polling versus interrupts; DMA in brief
Bus timing and wait states

units.title: Assembling, linking and debugging
topics: Two-pass assembly, symbol tables, object files, relocation and linking
Macros, conditional assembly and include files
Mixing C and assembly: inline assembly and calling assembly from C
Debugging: breakpoints, single-stepping, watching registers and memory, disassembly
Project: a complete program such as a calculator, a traffic-light controller or a text game on the simulator

schedule.title: Architecture, registers and the instruction cycle
schedule.exercise: Draw a block diagram of a CPU with its three buses and explain, in one paragraph, why a Harvard design can fetch an instruction and read data at the same time.

tasks.title: Step a three-instruction program one cycle at a time and record the program counter, accumulator and flags after each step in a table
Trace the fetch, decode and execute phases of an ADD instruction and label which registers and buses are active in each machine cycle
Given a trace of a faulty program that never halts, find the instruction whose fetch address is wrong and explain the corrupted program counter

schedule.title: Case processors and the toolchain
schedule.exercise: Write a short comparison table of x86, ARM Cortex-M and RISC-V (word size, register count, instruction length) and justify which one suits a low-cost lab kit.

tasks.title: Assemble and load a four-line program in the simulator, run it to completion and read the final register values from the debugger
Set a breakpoint, single-step a loop that sums 1 to 10 and watch the register that accumulates the total reach 55
Port a small add-and-store routine from one instruction set to the lab CPU and list every instruction that had to change and why

schedule.title: Instruction encoding and addressing modes
schedule.exercise: Hand-encode five instructions into binary and hex using the lab CPU's format table, then decode three machine words back into assembly.

tasks.title: Hand-encode a MOV, an ADD and a JMP instruction into 16-bit words, then load them into memory and confirm the CPU executes them as intended
Write one program that loads the same value using immediate, direct, register-indirect and indexed modes and compare the effective address each one uses
Decode a dump of eight unknown machine words into assembly, identify which fields are opcode, register and immediate, and predict the final register state

schedule.title: Data layout and array access
schedule.exercise: Explain why a 32-bit value stored at an odd address can be slow or illegal on some processors, with a worked memory diagram for both byte orders.

tasks.title: Store the 16-bit value 0x1234 at address 0x20 and read it back byte by byte to show which end of the word is stored first
Use indexed addressing to sum an array of ten bytes in memory and store the total, then verify it against a hand calculation
Access the fields of a record array holding a student id and score using base-plus-offset addressing, and find the highest score without using a fixed address

schedule.title: Data movement and arithmetic
schedule.exercise: Work through a problem set on signed versus unsigned results of ADD, SUB, MUL and DIV for 8-bit values and predict the carry and overflow flags before running.

tasks.title: Declare three data values with directives, load them into registers with MOV and store the sum back to memory, checking the memory window
Add two 32-bit numbers held in register pairs using ADD and ADC and confirm the carry propagates correctly with a result that overflows 16 bits
Compute the average of five unsigned test scores with MUL and DIV, then fix a version that gives a wrong answer when the sum exceeds 8 bits

schedule.title: Logic, flags and number conversion
schedule.exercise: Predict, on paper, the flag values after ten short instruction sequences, then check them against the simulator and explain any mismatch.

tasks.title: Use AND, OR and XOR with masks to set, clear and toggle individual bits of a status byte standing for relay outputs, and verify each result
Run a CMP between two numbers and show which flags are set, then use them to pick the larger value without any conditional jump
Write a routine that converts a 16-bit binary number into five printable ASCII decimal digits and test it with three values including 0 and 65535

schedule.title: Branches, loops and subroutines
schedule.exercise: Translate three short if-else and loop fragments from pseudocode into assembly on paper, then write the flowchart that matches each translation.

tasks.title: Translate an if-else that classifies a mark as pass or fail at 50 into compare and conditional jump instructions and test with four input values
Write a counted loop that multiplies two numbers by repeated addition and compare the number of cycles it needs with the MUL instruction
Write a subroutine that returns the maximum of an array passed by pointer and length, call it twice, and confirm the stack returns to its starting depth

schedule.title: Calling conventions, strings and compiler output
schedule.exercise: Read a small piece of compiler-generated assembly for a C function and annotate each instruction with the C statement it came from.

tasks.title: Write strlen in assembly for a zero-terminated string and test it with an empty string, a one-character string and a ten-character string
Implement a recursive factorial function with a stack frame per call and watch the stack grow and shrink as the recursion unwinds for input 5
Implement a bubble sort over eight bytes in memory, count the swaps performed, and then add an early-exit check to cut the passes on already sorted data

schedule.title: Stack and interrupt vectors
schedule.exercise: Draw the stack contents after a sequence of PUSH, CALL and POP instructions and explain what happens if RET is executed with the wrong value on top.

tasks.title: Push five values onto the stack, pop them back and show on the memory window that they come out in reverse order
Reserve space for two local variables on the stack using a frame pointer, use them in a function and release them before returning
Debug a program that crashes after a subroutine returns because of an unbalanced PUSH, locate the extra push by single-stepping and repair it

schedule.title: Interrupt service routines and system calls
schedule.exercise: Write a short design note on how a nested, prioritised interrupt system decides which handler runs first and what must be saved on entry.

tasks.title: Trigger a software interrupt, follow the CPU as it saves the flags and return address, runs the handler and resumes the main program
Write a timer interrupt handler that increments a tick counter every interrupt while the main loop runs, and show the counter rising independently
Handle two interrupt sources with different priorities so the higher one can pre-empt the lower, and demonstrate a nested interrupt in the trace

schedule.title: Memory map and parallel I/O
schedule.exercise: Design an address map for a small board with 4 KB of ROM and 2 KB of RAM and show the decoder equations for each chip select.

tasks.title: Build an address decoder from gates that selects a RAM chip for addresses 0x8000 to 0x87FF and test it with six sample addresses
Write to a memory-mapped output port address to light eight LEDs in a chasing pattern and read a switch port to reverse the direction
Drive a seven-segment display from a GPIO port to count from 0 to 9 and debug a version that shows wrong digits because of the segment table

schedule.title: Serial I/O, timing and polling versus interrupts
schedule.exercise: Compare polling and interrupt-driven input for a keypad in a prepaid meter, with a table of CPU utilisation and response delay for both.

tasks.title: Transmit the ASCII string HELLO through a simulated UART by polling the status flag before each byte and check the received characters
Read a key press once by polling and once by interrupt, and measure how many instruction cycles the CPU wastes in the polling version
Choose a UART baud rate divisor and delay loop for a 9600 baud link at the given clock, then verify the timing against the bit period in the trace

schedule.title: Assembly toolchain, debugging and project
schedule.exercise: Write a one-page design for a traffic-light controller or calculator in assembly, listing modules, memory use, test cases and a state diagram.

tasks.title: Use breakpoints, a watch window and the disassembly view to find a deliberately planted off-by-one error in a given array-copy routine
Perform a two-pass assembly by hand on a ten-line program with forward labels, build the symbol table and check it against the assembler listing
Build and test a traffic-light controller with a timer interrupt, a pedestrian request input and a state machine, and demonstrate all four phases in order
